ten_conversions.text:
When an agent promises work on an observed issue, render that promise as the GitHub assignee. Hugh's framing: a promise in the workroom should show up on the issue, so someone reading GitHub can see the work is claimed without being told.

This is rendering rather than a command. It projects durable state — who holds the live promise — onto a field the connector owns and nothing reads back, and it is naturally idempotent: re-rendering the same promise sets the same assignee. So it needs no ceremony of its own, unlike opening a pull request, which is a discrete side effect and goes through the work loop.

Two problems have to be settled first, and neither is incidental.

There is no mapping from a workroom actor to a GitHub account, and inventing one silently would be the dishonesty this connector exists to avoid. I checked: no actor in the roster carries a GitHub login — claude, codex, hugh and github-connector all carry name, kind, roles and membership only. Assigning the token's owner as a stand-in would be the worst available answer, because the issue would then say Hugh is working on something Claude promised, and the GitHub side would be asserting an attribution the log contradicts. The mapping has to be stated by someone with the authority to state it, and the charter is the natural place, since it already names the connector, owner, repository and actor and is already ratified. An actor with no mapping simply renders no assignee.

GitHub silently drops assignees it does not accept. The issues API accepts an `assignees` array, and usernames without push access to the repository are discarded without error — the call returns success and the issue ends up assigned to nobody. That is exactly the failure this workroom has spent the day chasing in its own log: an operation that reports success and means nothing. So the connector must read back what GitHub actually recorded and treat a dropped assignee as a failure rather than trusting the status code. A rendering that cannot confirm itself should say so rather than appear to have worked.

Worth deciding while implementing: what happens when the promise is superseded or the commitment is reneged. The honest rendering is to clear the assignee, since the field is a projection of current state rather than a history, and the log remains the record of who once promised.

ten_conversions.text:
Make "needs my action" include ratification, because the one obligation only Hugh can discharge is the one it cannot show.

Hugh reported that two things he was told he must do do not appear in the panel. Investigating gave three separate causes, and the third is the one worth fixing here.

One of the two was never filed durably at all — my failure, now filed. The other, the charter request 0fe20fcc, is a genuine open commitment addressed to his fingerprint and should appear; if it does not, the likely cause is that `me` is undefined, because WorkDrawer.tsx resolves it as the fingerprint of the actor whose name equals `session.actor` and only when exactly one configured actor matches. A browser session with no actor, or a name matching none or two, empties the panel silently for everyone.

The structural gap is this. `workItemNeedsAction` switches on `commitment.status` and nothing else, so the panel can only ever show commitments. Ratification is not a commitment. Right now the live log holds 8 unratified proposals and 39 unratified asserts, and Hugh holds the only `ratifier` role in the room — so his principal duty is exactly the population the panel is blind to. He has been finding it by being told in conversation, which is not a queue.

There is a second, smaller undercount beside it: `needsCount` sums over items inside topics, so a commitment whose root is not a topic is invisible. That is the same shape as the defect in the work counts fixed at 804bcd1f, where two of three figures were summed over topics while the third came from the projection.

Worth deciding rather than assuming: not every unratified act is owed to somebody. An assert usually stands on its author's signature and never needs ratification, so counting all 39 would be noise, and noise is how a signal stops being read. What is genuinely owed is narrower — kinds whose lifecycle requires ratification to take force, addressed to an actor holding the role that can give it. That distinction is the work.
